questions.stem: Read this stanza: 'The magpie warbles on the wire, / The paddock wakes in gold and green, / The kettle sings beside the fire, / The dew still sparkles, cold and clean.' What is its rhyme scheme?
options: AABB
ABBA
ABCB
ABAB
questions.explanation: Give each new end sound a letter: 'wire' is A, 'green' is B, 'fire' rhymes with 'wire' so it is A again, and 'clean' rhymes with 'green' so it is B. Alternating rhymes like this make ABAB. AABB would need the first two lines to rhyme with each other, as a pair.

questions.stem: Which line contains internal rhyme?
options: The wind blew hard across the plain
Softly the misty morning rain comes down
The river runs beside the road
The night was bright with silver light
questions.explanation: Internal rhyme places rhyming words inside a line, not just at the end: 'night', 'bright' and 'light' all rhyme within this one line. The river line repeats an 'r' sound, which is alliteration rather than rhyme. Internal rhyme adds a musical, quickening effect.

questions.stem: In poetry, metre is:
options: the pattern of rhyming words found at the ends of lines
the repetition of consonant sounds at the start of words
the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line
the number of lines contained in each separate stanza of a poem
questions.explanation: Metre is the measured beat of a poem, built from stressed and unstressed syllables arranged in a pattern. The pattern of end rhymes is the rhyme scheme, which is a separate feature. Repeating initial consonant sounds is alliteration.

questions.stem: An iamb is a unit of rhythm made of:
options: two stressed syllables side by side, as in 'heartbreak'
an unstressed syllable then a stressed one, as in 'today'
a stressed syllable then an unstressed one, as in 'garden'
two unstressed syllables then a stressed one, as in 'understand'
questions.explanation: An iamb goes da-DUM, as in to-DAY. 'Garden' is the reverse pattern, DUM-da, which is called a trochee. Say the word aloud and listen for which syllable is louder.

questions.stem: A line of iambic pentameter contains:
options: five lines, each ending with a rhyming word
five iambs, giving ten syllables in a da-DUM rhythm
five stressed syllables with no unstressed ones at all
four iambs, giving eight syllables in total
questions.explanation: 'Penta' means five, so iambic pentameter is five iambs in a row: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, ten syllables altogether. Four iambs would be iambic tetrameter. Shakespeare wrote most of his plays in this metre because it sounds close to natural English speech.

questions.stem: Which line is written in iambic pentameter?
options: Watching the tide as it rolls in over the sand
Tide comes, tide goes, sand sighs, sun sets
I watched the tide roll in across the sand
The tide rolls in across the sand
questions.explanation: Read the line aloud: i-WATCHED the-TIDE roll-IN a-CROSS the-SAND has ten syllables in five da-DUM pairs. The shorter version has only eight syllables, four iambs. 'Watching the tide' starts with a stressed syllable and has twelve syllables, so its rhythm is not iambic pentameter.

questions.stem: Blank verse is poetry written in:
options: rhyming couplets of any length
lines with no regular rhythm
three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables
unrhymed iambic pentameter
questions.explanation: Blank verse has a regular metre, iambic pentameter, but no rhyme; it is 'blank' because the line endings do not rhyme. Lines with no regular rhythm or rhyme are free verse, which is easily confused with blank verse. Much of Shakespeare's dialogue is blank verse.

questions.stem: What is free verse?
options: Poetry that must have exactly fourteen lines
Poetry written only about nature and seasons
Poetry that tells a story in rhyming stanzas
Poetry with no set rhyme scheme or metre
questions.explanation: Free verse is 'free' from fixed patterns of rhyme and metre, so the poet shapes rhythm through line breaks, repetition and the natural flow of speech. A fourteen-line form is a sonnet. Free verse can still be carefully crafted; it simply does not follow a set pattern.

questions.stem: Consonance is the repetition of:
options: vowel sounds repeated inside nearby words in a line
the same word at the start of each line
a whole line at the end of each stanza
consonant sounds within or at the end of words
questions.explanation: Consonance repeats consonant sounds, often within or at the end of words, as in 'the black truck struck the dock'. Repeating vowel sounds is assonance. Repeating a whole line at the end of each stanza is a refrain.

questions.stem: In the line 'He stopped. The bush was silent, still and dark,' what does the full stop after 'stopped' create?
options: Enjambment, where a line runs on to the next
A couplet, a pair of lines that rhyme together
A caesura, a pause in the middle of the line
A refrain, a line or phrase that is repeated
questions.explanation: A caesura is a break or pause within a line of poetry, often marked by punctuation such as a full stop. Here the sudden stop mirrors the character freezing. Enjambment is the opposite effect: a sentence flows over the end of a line without a pause.

questions.stem: In a ballad or song, a refrain is:
options: lines repeated at intervals, often after each stanza
the first line of the poem, which introduces its subject
a pause in the middle of a line, marked by punctuation
the final couplet that sums up the argument of a sonnet
questions.explanation: A refrain returns again and again, like the chorus of a song, which makes a poem memorable and builds emphasis each time it comes back. A pause in the middle of a line is a caesura. Refrains are common in ballads because they were made to be sung or recited aloud.

questions.stem: A stanza of four lines is called a:
options: tercet
couplet
sonnet
quatrain
questions.explanation: A quatrain has four lines, a tercet three and a couplet two. A sonnet is a whole fourteen-line poem, not a stanza. Quatrains are the most common stanza in English poetry, including many Australian bush ballads.

questions.stem: How many lines does a traditional sonnet have?
options: Sixteen
Ten
Fourteen
Twelve
questions.explanation: A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem, traditionally written in iambic pentameter. Its two main traditional versions divide those fourteen lines in different ways, but both keep the total of fourteen.

questions.stem: How does a Shakespearean sonnet usually end?
options: With a refrain repeated word for word from the opening line
With one unrhymed line that stands alone as its own stanza
With a rhyming couplet that sums up or twists the argument
With six lines answering a question raised in the first eight
questions.explanation: A Shakespearean sonnet is three quatrains followed by a final rhyming couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. The two lines at the end often deliver the turn or the conclusion. An eight-line section followed by six lines is the pattern of a Petrarchan sonnet.

questions.stem: In a sonnet, the volta is:
options: the turn, where the poem shifts in argument or mood
the opening line, which names the subject of the poem
the steady rhythm of ten syllables in every line
the pattern of rhymes across all fourteen lines
questions.explanation: Volta is Italian for 'turn'. It is the point where the sonnet changes direction, for example from a problem to a solution, or from praise to doubt. In a Petrarchan sonnet it usually comes at line nine; in a Shakespearean sonnet it often comes in the final couplet.

questions.stem: A Petrarchan sonnet is divided into:
options: seven rhyming couplets of equal length
two equal stanzas of seven lines each
an eight-line octave and a six-line sestet
three quatrains and a final rhyming couplet
questions.explanation: The Petrarchan, or Italian, sonnet opens with an eight-line octave that usually sets out a problem, then turns in a six-line sestet that responds to it. Three quatrains and a couplet is the Shakespearean pattern, which is the most common confusion between the two forms.

questions.stem: In English, a traditional haiku has:
options: three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, often on nature
fourteen lines, often about love and written in rhyme
five lines with a humorous AABBA rhyme scheme
any number of lines and no rules about length
questions.explanation: Haiku come from Japan, and in English they are usually written as three lines of five, seven and five syllables, capturing a single moment in nature. A five-line comic poem rhyming AABBA is a limerick. A fourteen-line poem is a sonnet.

questions.stem: A student writes a haiku about cicadas buzzing on a hot afternoon. Including the cicadas follows which haiku tradition?
options: Telling a long story with a clear beginning and end
Exaggerating for comic effect, as a limerick does
Using a seasonal word to place the poem in time
Ending with a rhyming couplet that states a moral
questions.explanation: Traditional Japanese haiku include a kigo, a word or image that signals the season, and cicadas immediately suggest an Australian summer. Haiku are very short and do not tell long stories or end with a moral. The seasonal word lets a few syllables call up a whole scene.

questions.stem: Which form is a short, humorous five-line poem with an AABBA rhyme scheme?
options: Elegy
Ode
Free verse
Limerick
questions.explanation: A limerick has five lines: the first, second and fifth rhyme and are longer, while the shorter third and fourth lines rhyme with each other. Limericks are almost always comic. An elegy is a serious poem of mourning, the opposite in tone.

questions.stem: A poem written to mourn the death of a grandfather is best called:
options: an ode
a limerick
an epic
an elegy
questions.explanation: An elegy is a reflective poem of grief for someone who has died. An ode praises or celebrates a person, object or idea, which can be confused with an elegy because both often honour someone. An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds.

questions.stem: An ode is a poem that:
options: tells a story in short stanzas with a refrain
uses exactly seventeen syllables in three lines
addresses and praises a person, object or idea
mourns the death of someone the poet loved
questions.explanation: An ode is a poem of celebration, often speaking directly to its subject, such as an ode to the ocean or to a favourite pair of boots. Mourning someone is the job of an elegy. Seventeen syllables in three lines describes a haiku.

questions.stem: Which features are typical of a traditional ballad?
options: It tells a story in quatrains, often with a refrain
It is fourteen lines long and has a clear volta
It has three short lines and no rhyme or regular beat
It is unrhymed and has no regular rhythm
questions.explanation: Ballads are narrative poems, originally sung, so they use simple rhyming quatrains, a strong beat and often a refrain. Australian bush ballads follow this tradition. A fourteen-line poem with a volta is a sonnet.

questions.stem: What most sets slam or spoken-word poetry apart from other poetry?
options: It is written to be performed aloud, using voice and gesture
It must follow a strict fourteen-line rhyme scheme and metre
It is only ever published in printed collections for reading
It avoids personal or political subjects in favour of nature
questions.explanation: Spoken-word poetry is designed for performance, so the poet's voice, pace, pauses and body language are part of the poem. It usually has no fixed form at all. Slam poems are often personal or political, which is part of their energy.

questions.stem: In a play, an aside is:
options: a written instruction in the script telling actors how to move
a brief remark to the audience that other characters cannot hear
a long speech in which a character alone on stage reveals their thoughts
a long speech that one character delivers to other characters on stage
questions.explanation: An aside is a quick comment, often a single line, shared with the audience while the other characters carry on as if they heard nothing. A long speech by a character alone on stage is a soliloquy. Asides let the audience in on secrets, which often creates dramatic irony.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a soliloquy and a monologue?
options: A soliloquy is a single line; a monologue must last at least ten minutes
In a soliloquy the character is alone or unheard; a monologue usually addresses others
A soliloquy is always written in rhyme; a monologue is always written in prose
A soliloquy is always spoken by the villain; a monologue is always spoken by the hero
questions.explanation: Both are long speeches by one character, but a soliloquy reveals private thoughts as if no one else can hear, while a monologue is usually addressed to other characters. Either can be in verse or prose, and either can be spoken by any character. Ask who is meant to be listening.

questions.stem: In a script, the words '(She slams the door and sits, shaking.)' are:
options: a line of dialogue
a soliloquy
stage directions
an aside
questions.explanation: Stage directions tell actors and directors what happens on stage: movements, actions, tone and setting. They are not spoken aloud, which is why they are usually in brackets or italics. Dialogue is the words characters actually say.

questions.stem: In ancient Greek drama, the chorus was:
options: a set of notes in the script telling actors where to stand
a group who commented on the action, often in song
the main character, whose fatal flaw brought about their downfall
the final scene, in which the conflict was settled at last
questions.explanation: The chorus was a group of performers who described events, reacted to them and drew out the moral, often in song. The main character whose flaw leads to their downfall is the tragic hero. Some modern plays and films still use a chorus-like narrator.

questions.stem: In a tragedy, hamartia is:
options: the chorus's final speech, delivered to the audience
the tragic hero's flaw or error that leads to their downfall
the happy ending in which the lovers marry and all is forgiven
the moment the audience laughs at a character's mistake
questions.explanation: Hamartia is a Greek term for the flaw or mistake, such as pride, jealousy or ambition, that brings a tragic hero down. A happy ending with lovers united belongs to comedy, not tragedy. The flaw matters because it makes the downfall partly the hero's own doing.

questions.stem: In a play, a respected general's jealousy leads him to believe a lie, destroying his marriage and his own life. Why is he called a tragic hero?
options: He is an evil character whom the audience is glad to see punished
He is a comic figure whose mistakes are all fixed by the end
He is destroyed by bad luck that has nothing to do with his choices
He is admirable, yet a flaw in him brings about his own downfall
questions.explanation: A tragic hero begins as someone we respect, and a flaw in their character, here jealousy, leads to their ruin. They are not simply a villain, because the audience feels pity for them as they fall. Pure bad luck would make the story sad, but not a tragedy in this sense.
